Confirmed. This shows the register corrupted:

```
        fprintf(stderr, "REMAPPING BRANCH REGISTERS\n");
        fprintf(stderr, "  +++ BEFORE R0 = %p\n", (void*)(regs.ref[0].ptr)); \
        iree_vm_bytecode_dispatch_remap_branch_registers(regs_i32, regs_ref,
                                                         remap_list);
        fprintf(stderr, "  +++ AFTER R0 = %p\n", (void*)(regs.ref[0].ptr)); \
```

Suspected off by one. For this stack frame, we have:

```
I32 REGISTER COUNT = 0xf28, REF COUNT = 0x33d
```

But we are remapping into 0xf28, which overlaps with ref storage by 1. Given alignment, this is clobbering the low order 32bits of the ref.

Oh man, it just so happens that this model generates control flow such that the highest numbered register in the program (`%i3880`) is *only* the source or target of a branch remapping and is not used in normal execution. Both the allocator and the verifier are missing this case, and since it is the highest numbered register in the program, it results in an off by one against allocated integer storage.

Ok, the correct fix is a bit involved, but applying a gross hack gets us on to the next issue:

In BytecodeEncoder.cpp:425, we just artificially inflate the number of registers to allocate (since this happens to be compiling to use one more than needed, this "works").
```
  result.i32RegisterCount = registerAllocation.getMaxI32RegisterOrdinal() + 50;
  result.refRegisterCount = registerAllocation.getMaxRefRegisterOrdinal() + 50;
```

But it appears to work with llvm-cpu and is producing real numbers.

[64bit_remap_repro.zip](https://github.com/openxla/iree/files/11973998/64bit_remap_repro.zip)

The above contains an illegal vmfb that should fail the verifier once it is fixed. At head, the compiler will no longer generate illegal register allocations, so preserving here so that we can strengthen the runtime against future issues. This has branches in it that reference remapped i32 register ordinals one past the declared number of registers for the function.

oh, right, this would be the reason why the verifier wasn't erroring....
```c
#define IREE_VM_VERIFY_REG_ANY(ordinal)                             \
  if (IREE_UNLIKELY(((ordinal)&IREE_REF_REGISTER_TYPE_BIT) == 0)) { \
  } else {                                                          \
  }
```
Yeah... And that bit gets used in two paths and only one of them has access to the function level limits. (Iirc)

Oh man, it just so happens that this model generates control flow such that the highest numbered register in the program (`%i3880`) is *only* the source or target of a branch remapping and is not used in normal execution. Both the allocator and the verifier are missing this case, and since it is the highest numbered register in the program, it results in an off by one against allocated integer storage.

issue.body:
Currently, if a branch remapping includes 64bit ints, it depends on the topology of the program as to whether enough scratch space happens to be available. In a case tested, it was not. This is because remappings are done 32bits at a time and presume that scratch space has been reserved for each word. This last part was not being done, resulting in the possibility of declared i32 register capacities to be off by the number of 64bit remappings in any CFG.

Fixes the runtime crash in #14313 by generating proper code. However, additional runtime hardening work is needed:

* The verifier is presently not verifying remapped register ordinals at all.
* Even if verification is enabled for this, it does not trigger because it is verifying that they are in range of the maximum allowable (vs declared).
* There should be padding between the i32/ref register storage areas, and ASAN marking should be done to catch any overflows.

issue.body:
This enables branch and variadic operand verification. It only verifies that the referenced registers are in the declared range and that there will be no out-of-bounds access of the register files at runtime. It will not catch correctness issues (but the verifier isn't intended to).

Fixes #14313.
